parole.significato: A member of the Sioux tribe of American Indian; Siouan.
parole.testo: Probably from Ojibwe Ab-Boin-Og (“Dakota; Sioux; roasters (From their habit of torturing people)”)/ᐊᑉ ᐳᐃᓐ ᐅᒃ

parole.significato: An Ojibwe, Nipissing, Algonquin, Potawatomi, or Odawa person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe anishinaabe /ᐊᓂᔑᓈᐯ. Doublet of Nishnaabe (from Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe) and Neshnabé (from Potawatomi).

parole.significato: An evil sorcerer, specifically one who walks by night in the form of a bear.
parole.testo: Calque of Ojibwe me'coubmoosa (“bear walker”).

parole.significato: Any of certain the small, striped rodents, all found in North America, with the exception of the Siberian chipmunk, pla…
parole.testo: 1832; alteration (influenced by chipping squirrel) of earlier chitmunk, from older Ojibwe ačitamo˙nˀ (“squirrels”) (modern ajidamoo), literally ‘those who descend headlong’, from ačit- (“headfirst, face-down”) (compare modern ajijibizo (“he falls headfirst”), ajidagoojin (“he hangs upside down”)). parole.significato: A member of the Ojibwe people.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe ojibwe (“Ojibwe”)/ᐅᒋᑉᐌ, specifically an eastern dialect with a reduced initial vowel. Compare earlier Ojibwa. Attested in English from the mid 18th century.

parole.significato: A First Nations mixed tribe of Plains Cree, Saulteaux and Métis.
parole.testo: * From Ojibwe Ka-wezauce . Literally, “Little Boy”; the name of the chief. * The tribe and the place were named after the chief.

parole.significato: High-proof alcoholic beverage, especially whiskey (especially in the context of its sale to or consumption by Native Am…
parole.testo: A calque of a Native American language term, probably Ojibwe ishkodewaaboo (“alcohol”), from ishkodew- (“fire”) + -aaboo (“liquid”, glossed in older works as “water”). parole.significato: White people or (more recently) any non-native people.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe zhaaganaash/ᔖᑲᓈᐦᔑᐝ (“white person”).

parole.significato: A prophet or medicine man among certain Native American peoples.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe, likely Ojibwe jaasakiid, third person singular subject changed conjunct of jiisakii (“s/he operates a shaking tent”).

parole.significato: A member of Kiwanis International, an international service club founded in 1915 in Detroit, Michigan.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe [Term?] (“we trade”).

parole.significato: An underskirt worn by some Native American girls and women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe majigoodenh (“dress”), from Proto-Algonquian *-iko·tay (“skirt”), with an empty prefix and contemptive suffix.

parole.significato: A heavy woolen cloth.
parole.testo: Respelling of Mackinac, a strait between Lake Huron and Lake Michigan, an island in the strait, and an important trading-post on the island; ultimately from Ojibwe mishinii-makinaang (“at the place of many snapping turtles”).

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed cargo boat, resembling a canoe, often schooner-rigged, formerly used on the Great Lakes and the Missour…
parole.testo: From Ojibwe.

parole.significato: A mackinaw coat.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe.

parole.significato: A cargo boat, with a large flat bottom and sharp ends, formerly used on the Great Lakes and the Missouri River (to a le…
parole.testo: From Ojibwe.

parole.significato: The lake trout or North American lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush).
parole.testo: From Ojibwe [Term?].

parole.significato: wild rice, usually northern wild rice (Zizania palustris)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe manoomin, from Proto-Algonquian *maθo·mina. Doublet of mnomen, which is from Potawatomi, and Mahnomen, a placename.

parole.significato: A Native American shamanistic healer.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of Ojibwe mashkikiiwinini (“doctor”), from mashkiki (“medicine”) + inini (“man”).

parole.significato: A female Native American (or, any other indigenous) shamanistic healer.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of Ojibwe mashkikiiwininiikwe (“female doctor”), from mashkiki (“medicine”) + inini (“man”) + ikwe (“woman”).

parole.significato: A member of a nation of Native Americans indigenous to what is now Wisconsin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe manoominii (literally “wild-rice people”); from Ojibwe manoomin.

parole.significato: A deke consisting of lifting the puck with the stick and throwing it under the top corner of the goal, while skating be…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe mishi-gami / ᒥᔑᑲᒥ (“giant lake”), referring to Lake Michigan.

parole.significato: Used in a common chronometric counting scheme, in which each iteration is sequentially numbered and supposed to equal a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe misi-ziibi, ᒥᓯ᐀ᓰᐱ (misi-siipi, “great river”).

parole.significato: A woven bag traditionally used by certain tribes native to northeastern North America.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe mashkimod (“bag, sack”), Plains Cree maskimot / Cree ᒪᐢᑭᒧᐟ (maskimot, “bag”).

parole.significato: A member of the Nipissing First Nation, a people of Ojibwa and Algonquin descent whose ancestors lived in the area of L…
parole.testo: From Ojibwe nibiinsing (“at-the-little-waters”), from nibyi- (“water”) + -ns (diminutive forming suffix) + -ing (locative forming suffix).

parole.significato: A Native North American.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe niijii (“my friend”); its further origin is not entirely clear. Eugene Stillday says it is a short form of niijikiwenh (“my brother, my fellow man”). Also from Cree [Term?].

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to this people, culture or language.
parole.testo: First attested in English around 1700 (and attested in early French as Outchibouec), from the Ojibwe name of an individual band of Ojibwe, of unclear origin. parole.significato: A member of the Ottawa people.
parole.testo: From Ojibwe odaawaa/ᐅᑡᐙ (“an Ottawa; a trader”), from Proto-Algonquian *atawewa (“to trade”).

parole.significato: A member of a Native American people of the upper Mississippi River region.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe boodawaadamii or Potawatomi Bodéwademi (“those who tend the fire”) (unsyncoped form of Bodéwadmi), from boodawaadam/bodewadm (“hearth”).

parole.significato: A freshwater fish from Lake Superior in the Great Lakes, a variety of the lake trout.
parole.testo: From an Ojibwe word, given by some English dictionaries as pemitewiskawet ("fish with oily meat") (compare bimide (“grease”), -skaw- (“meat of a fish”), -e (“an incorporating final”)), perhaps via French ciscoette.

parole.significato: The full moon in June closest to the summer solstice.
parole.testo: A calque of Ojibwe ode'imini-giizis (“strawberry moon”), because June is strawberry season.

parole.significato: Any natural object or living creature that serves as an emblem of a tribe, clan or family; the representation of such a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe (o)doodem(an).

parole.significato: A Native North American bisexual, homosexual, or gender-variant person; especially one belonging to a traditional triba…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from two + spirit, coined in 1990 at the Third Annual Inter-tribal Native American, First Nations, Gay and Lesbian American Conference held in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada, based on Ojibwe niizh manidoowag (“two spirits”) (coined at the same conference), from niizh (“two”) + manido

parole.significato: The root of the spruce, and sometimes also of the pine, split lengthwise into strips and used in the construction of ba…
parole.testo: From Ojibwe wadab (“a spruce root”).

parole.significato: A malevolent and violent cannibal spirit found in Anishinaabe, Ojibwe, and Cree mythology, which is said to inhabit the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ojibwe wiindigoo, from Proto-Algonquian *wi·nteko·wa (“owl; malevolent spirit, cannibalistic monster”). Compare Plains Cree wîhtikow, ᐃᐧᐦᑎᑯᐤ (“greedy person; cannibal; giant man-eating monster”).
